objectAssessments.reasoning: The English preserves reproducible unit conventions and distinguishes changed numerical representation from unchanged physical laws. It does not turn unit choice into arbitrary changes of the law.

Conditional net-charge leakage and the limitation of a lasting material standard are retained, without claiming precise charge measurement is impossible or presenting the old meter analogy as current SI. Negative electron charge, positive elementary-charge magnitude and Coulomb-era history remain distinct.

The electrostatic unit uses two equal point charges in vacuum at 1 centimeter with force magnitude 1 dyne, and preserves 10^-5 newton. The k=1 convention is attached to the simultaneous charge, length and force units, not imposed on SI or other unit systems.
The introduction correctly restricts the following magnitude formula to the defined electrostatic units, point charges and vacuum. It does not introduce a material-medium coefficient.
Formula 8-3 retains both absolute charge values and inverse-square distance. In its surrounding electrostatic context F is magnitude, not a signed directional force.

CGSE remains the textbook designation for the absolute electrostatic charge unit in the centimeter-gram-second electrostatic system. The English explicitly says e is magnitude, not the negative signed electron charge.
The retained 4.8 x 10^-10 CGSE value is identified as the original rounded value. No exact modern defining-value claim has been added.

The historical current-carrying-wire method is expressly separated from the present elementary-charge-and-second ampere definition. The coulomb relation requires a steady 1 ampere for 1 second; varying current needs interval charge rather than one instantaneous sample. The nearby cross-section context keeps that quantity as transported charge, and the 3 x 10^9 conversion is approximate.
Formula 8-4 and its numerical conversion are preserved with an explicit warning that the rounded equality is not an exact unit definition. There is no silent replacement of textbook precision.

The same-sign 1-coulomb, 1-kilometer vacuum point-charge comparison retains the mass as 1 metric ton, not a US short ton. Difficulty retaining net charge is conditional on ordinary isolated objects and environments, not universal impossibility. Cumulative charge through a conductor is not its net stored charge. The 100-watt/127-volt bulb is a rated-power/rated-voltage estimate, explicitly not a practical learner operation.
The elementary charge remains the positive quantity e. The introduction distinguishes the textbook approximation from the complete significant digits in the present defining value.
Formula 8-5 retains 1.6 x 10^-19 coulomb as the approximation introduced immediately above, not the signed electron charge or an exact number.

The k rearrangement and newton times meter-squared per coulomb-squared dimension are preserved. The warning to compare coefficient numbers with their units prevents confusing k's numerical value across unit systems.
The calculation still concerns two point charges in vacuum, each 1 coulomb and 1 meter apart, using CGSE units. The 1-kilometer comparison has not been substituted into this separate example.

Both 3 x 10^9 charge conversions and denominator 10^4 remain exact to the approved formula. The text explains that the original 1-meter distance is converted to centimeters then squared, not physically changed.
The dyne-to-newton conversion and 9 x 10^9 newton result are preserved. The English limits precision to that of the textbook's rounded constants.

The same physical force, not an identical numerical force across differently sized units, is represented in SI. The coefficient 9 x 10^9 with N*m^2/C^2 dimension remains tied to the lesson's approximate precision.

The substitution retains both 1-coulomb factors, the squared 1-meter denominator and 9 x 10^9 newton result. The math-literal changes to C and m only name the same units; they do not change variables, exponents or charge values.
The transition still identifies the coefficient for the just-described unit system and example, without introducing a new numerical claim.
The coefficient and dimension are preserved. The English explicitly describes 9 x 10^9 as a convenient approximation, not an exactly defined constant.
The next formula is introduced as another way of writing the same coefficient. No different physical interaction or coefficient is asserted.
Formula 8-6 retains k=1/(4*pi*epsilon0), including every factor and operator. It remains the vacuum-permittivity form of the SI coefficient.

Vacuum permittivity and the original electric-constant name denote the same quantity. The present numerical value is described as experimentally determined, while the lesson's following value is approximate; the English does not claim an exact modern definition.

Formula 8-7 preserves the previously approved terminal charge-square correction and all numerical values, equality signs and factors. Both displayed unit factors are C^2/(N*m^2), the inverse dimension of k. The 8.85 x 10^-12 number is still expressly the textbook approximation, not exact arithmetic with an exact 9 x 10^9 coefficient.
The transition introduces the SI law written with vacuum permittivity. It neither replaces vacuum with a material medium nor omits the final formula.

Formula 8-8 retains magnitude F, absolute charge values and inverse-square separation. Direction remains a separate same-sign-repulsion/opposite-sign-attraction statement. The English explicitly limits application to stationary vacuum charges treatable as point charges and rejects unconditional use for macroscopic media or arbitrary distributions.
